# Electric telegraph (`electric_telegraph`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/electricity.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Electricity & electronics (`electricity`)
- Deps: needs electric_battery; helped by electromagnetism, practical_batteries, ohms_law_circuits, wire_drawing, optical_telegraph
- Core idea: A key at one end closes a battery circuit; at the far end the current works an electromagnet that clicks, or deflects a needle. Letters are sent as patterns of short and long currents (Morse code, with the shortest signs for the most frequent letters). One iron or copper wire on poles is enough if it is carried on glass or glazed ceramic insulators and the circuit is completed through plates buried in the earth at both ends. For long lines a relay, a sensitive electromagnet that switches a fresh local battery, repeats the signal every few hundred kilometres.
- Pitfalls:
  - Wire fixed to wet wooden poles without insulators: in rain the current leaks to earth and nothing arrives
  - Believing two wires are always needed; the earth return (Steinheil, 1838) halves the cost
  - Too few cells for the line: resistance grows with length, so use thicker wire, more cells in series, or relays
  - No agreed code, operating rules and message accounting; the system is as much organisation as apparatus
  - Crediting Morse alone: needle telegraphs ran earlier in Germany, Russia and England, and the relay and much of the code came from Henry and Vail
- History: europe: 1809 – Sömmerring's electrochemical telegraph (Munich); 1832 Schilling's needle telegraph (St Petersburg); 1833 Gauss and Weber link observatory and laboratory in Göttingen; 1837 Cooke and Wheatstone patent, in commercial railway use from 1839; americas: 1837–1838 – Morse and Vail demonstrate their recording telegraph; 1844 Washington–Baltimore line; india: 1839 – O'Shaughnessy's experimental line near Calcutta; 1851–1854 first trunk lines; global: 1866 – lasting transatlantic cable; by the 1870s Europe, India, China, Australia and the Americas are linked
- Read:
  - Tom Standage, The Victorian Internet (1998)
  - Ken Beauchamp, History of Telegraphy (2001)
